title: Create or Modify System Process: Container Service
shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Container Service
summary: Container platforms run their own long-lived services on the host, and those services can be configured to start workloads automatically. On a single host, Docker and Podman run as daemons, and a container started with a restart policy such as restart=always is brought back by the daemon after a reboot or a crash, so the container becomes a persistent process that no login triggers. Where the parent technique installs a service, this sub-technique instead configures the container platform, so the lasting artefact is a container or workload definition rather than a service binary path. The security problem is wider than persistence: access to a rootful container command is close to root on the host, because a container can be started with host filesystem mounts, host network, or privileged mode and then used to modify the host itself. In a Kubernetes cluster the equivalent leverage comes from workload objects rather than host services. A DaemonSet places a pod on every node and keeps placing it on nodes added later, and a pod spec can be pinned to chosen nodes using nodeSelector or nodeName. Containers are also frequently wrapped as systemd units. Detection looks at container creation parameters, restart policies, privileged and host-mount flags, image provenance, and audit logs for pod and DaemonSet creation.

beginner.definition: One system process is a program that a computer starts by itself and keeps running in the background. Modern containers work the same way, because software like Docker and the agent inside a Kubernetes node also runs as a long-lived service. Containers run applications in small sealed boxes, and this technique abuses the settings that start those boxes again automatically.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who controls a container service can make their container restart after every reboot without logging in again. Containers often get special access to the machine they run on, so this also opens the door to privilege escalation. In a cluster, one setting can place their workload on many machines at once. Busy teams rarely review these settings by hand.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a container from an image they control, or replaces the image a workload already uses.
They add a restart policy such as restart=always, so the container returns after a crash or reboot.
They may request privileged mode, host network, or a host folder mount to reach the machine itself.
On Kubernetes, a DaemonSet style workload runs their pod on every node, including nodes added later.
The pod specification can also be pinned to chosen nodes using nodeSelector or nodeName fields.
Many teams wrap the container in a systemd unit, so it also starts like any other Linux service.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where guests never check out in person. Instead, every room can be booked to renew itself each night forever. A visitor books a room this way, so the front desk quietly rebooks it every evening. The hotel keeps paying for cleaning and power, and the guest keeps the key without ever visiting reception again.
takeaways: A container with a restart policy behaves like a service and survives reboots by design.
Rootful container access is close to root on the host, so treat it as a privileged position.
Cluster workload objects such as DaemonSets can spread an attacker's container across many nodes.

objectives: Explain how container restart policies create persistence on a host.
Describe why access to a rootful container command can mean host compromise.
Explain how DaemonSets and node selectors place workloads across a cluster.
Identify the log sources that record container and pod creation.
Distinguish legitimate deployment activity from unauthorised workload changes.
